claims.text: Successful nanoparticle high-entropy alloy formation occurs when all metal precursors reduce simultaneously.
Simultaneous reduction ensures nucleation and growth in a homogeneous, single-phase environment.
The proposed precursor solution contains salts of Pt, Pd, Rh, Ru, and Ir.
A strong reducing agent and appropriately chosen coordination ligands can balance the reduction behavior of the five metal precursors.
Balancing the reduction behavior will synchronize reduction of all metal ions at 80–120 °C.
Reducing-agent concentration and ligand environment can be tuned to match the reduction kinetics of all metal components.
Synchronized reduction produces homogeneous nucleation of all constituent metals.
Synchronized reduction produces congruent growth of all constituent metals.
Nearly simultaneous reduction causes nucleation events for the different metals to occur concurrently.
Concurrent nucleation kinetically locks the elements into a single solid-solution phase.
Kinetic locking occurs before thermodynamically driven phase separation or elemental segregation can take place.
The synchronized one-pot process will yield ultrafine high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The resulting nanoparticles will have uniformly mixed compositions, high surface-atom exposure, and minimal phase segregation.
Staggered reduction leads to phase separation, compositional gradients, and defect-rich interfaces.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal high-entropy systems synthesized under controlled, moderate-temperature, balanced reducing conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when extreme thermal inputs dominate.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when ligand and solvent environments cannot enforce synchronized reduction.
Minor ligand-coordination deviations or reduction-potential mismatches may prevent perfect synchronization.
The exact degree of reduction synchronicity is uncertain without real-time kinetic monitoring.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in compositional uniformity, phase purity, and morphology relative to the staggered-reduction baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
